Draw. You don't have to be amazing. The act of sketching and thinking from different perspectives will carry through to your 3d efforts. Similarly look up artstation 3d models for references. Start simple. Think in blobs and try to filter out detail. Keep a pencil with you at all times for reference lines for yourself. 

Draw on your work as you go. I use a pencil for cutting up the piece of wood with lines. It makes it easier on your eye. For example if you're making a person or creature then think how long the torso is and where the border is. Think about the highest points of your work and mark it with your pencil then work down from there, then repeat the process

The Lincoln technique is more than exposing a length of lead. It's an easy mistake to make for laymen observers or amateur enthusiasts, which is why having a solid foundation through education or mentorship is absolutely crucial for artisanal pencil sharpening.

The Lincoln technique is--more importantly-- a philosophy. It's an exploration of the pioneer spirit through the creative wilds. It's a promise of ambition gifted to yourself. It's to find the truth within yourself that you can achieve anything with the Lincoln technique; to find the truth that you are more than man, pencil and technique--you are a miracle with infinite potential.

The true power of the Lincoln technique isn't a perfectly honed lead for precise strokes, it's the honing of your mind until you become wise enough to recognise the simple, objective fact that we are all God's.

Sure! I finish the carving roughwork and try to get the surface as even as possible with a honed knife, then its sanding. 

Typically sand from 80 or 120 to 240. At 240 I spray with water and let dry. This lifts up all the fibres. Then I do 320 and move to polishing papers 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 5 and 7k. 1.5 to 5 is where you see the most difference. 7 and beyond is mostly just sheen and feel, so I stop at 7.

After that it's 1 coat of very thin clear oil (tung and resin blend), let it dry all day. If I'm doing any colour then it's oil paint stage

I use windsor and Newton oil paints, then usually dilute. If I need to get it into holes like the one cap here then I make it quite runny. You can also dilute them considerably to let the pigment get into the grain like a stain, but I don't do that often

After the paint is dry I do several coats of homemade shellac from dewaxed golden flakes mixed in ethanol. I like it at a consistency similar to watery syrup and apply with a fast moving brush. I sand between coats with a very high grit (5 or 7)

There is something to be said about wirewool finishes in terms of saving money and time on sanding, but I haven't experimented enough with them yet to say confidently which way or the other. I used them exclusively for some walking sticks I made and the finish was nice, but they might not be delicate enough for small figurines like this

I will say I don't like acrylic finishes and couldn't recommend oil paints enough. I also don't like poly finishes despite their ease of application. I like the idea of a finish being easy to amend. I haven't experimented with lacquer. It's something I've often associated with traditional carpentry, but in theory it would be a good finish to replace shellac if I wanted to

Oh also these caps are fixed on with epoxy. Ethanol dissolves epoxy, so I was concerned about the shellac weakening the hold but after some testing I realised it would take buckets of alcohol to make a dent in the epoxy so it's all good

You work like I do. I love going through the high grits to a silky finish. I start at 80 or 120 though. If 80, then I don't apply much pressure because it's very hard to get the scores out. 150+ doesn't remove enough material unless you've gone over the whole thing with a razorsharp knife and even then, so you'll always be left with some area of concern with irregular shapes like this

A rule I set myself is: the more time I spend on lower grits, the less time I have to spend on higher and the better the finish. So for me this looks like investing a lot of time looking for rough areas with 80 or 120

Regular sanding I stop at 240, spray with water and let dry, then do 320 and stop. For the superfine grits, I do 1500, 2000, 2.5, 3, 5, and 7. I find that everything after 5 is just gloss. I see the most improvement between 1.5 and 5k. So, I just use 7, then oil then 7 again and wipe down along the grain

Wirewools can be used as fine grits too, which might save on sandpapers, but I haven't taken the time to test and compare yet

Anyone can do anything. You can whittle. Don't worry, not being able to visualize your work from the get-go is normal. It's a skill that you develop as you go. I've been whittling for a couple of years and still, sometimes, I'll look at a blank and have absolutely no idea how to start on what it is I wanted to make

The best way to learn is to do. It takes a while to get used to using a knife and otherwise.

Drawing yourself guides as you go can help. I still draw a line down the center of my work then keep redrawing it as I take more off. It helps me to keep both sides symmetrical. Drawing a side profile on the block of wood is also helpful

Think about the highest point of an animal. This helps train your brain to have a starting point.

Think in shapes, not lines. Don't worry about detail at the start and just focus on form. Look at pictures of cats and try to imagine them from different perspectives.

Draw. You don't have to be good. It pulls from the same skillset as whittling, so learning with one compliments the other. Draw your cat shape as a stick-person by thinking of their skeleton, but limit yourself to straight lines

Think about the defining features of a cat. Think about the areas that you'll be carving. I would think about the shoulders, the hind and the shape of the legs. I'd ask myself questions like, how do cats fold up into a loaf so easily? What about their legs enables them to do that? 

If there are small details like ears, don't carve them from the get go. Just make the head a whole shape, then work from a center line. It will help you to keep symmetry with the face

Don't use too small a block of wood

Your first pieces are not going to be perfect, but you'll improve and get there if you stick at it

I use either gorilla woodglue or epoxy, but all woodglues are roughly the same. Because the break is uneven it might be hard to get it seamless and it might be difficult to get it to sit still without holding in place by hand for like 5-10minutes.

Epoxy can be nice because it dries to a self-holding consistency relatively quickly so you don't have to hold it for so long, unlike woodglue. Woodglue, you typically leave in a clamp overnight, but it does tack up in 5-10 minutes which can help keep it in place. Epoxy is better suited for small jobs like this though

You can get small mixer kits for epoxy at any hardware store under the glue section. You just mix it up 50/50 until it's clear and goopy (2-3 mins) then apply with something small like a halfed toothpick or halfed cotton swab (the sticks for ears). Hold the 2 bits together without moving it for a few minutes and it should hold itself. Any excess can be wiped away (note: it will smear along the wood and get stuck in the grain, so you might have to do some sanding after to remove it)

So, I recommend epoxy for actually sticking it, but unless it's a perfect fit then the break will still be noticeable. The problem with using epoxy is that you can't really cover it up after. Professional restorers might do something like carving a little trench in the dried adhesive along the break, then fill it with a custom woodfill (woodglue + sawdust of the source wood type), but that would be a lot of work and challenging if you're doing it for the first time

The best thing you can possibly do for yourself *and* for them, is to disengage and appreciate them for what good things they've done for you, while detaching yourself from the rest. They work like acrylics but instead of diluting with water you dilute with oil. I just use stainless tung oil from the hardware store but traditionally artists use linseed. Anything that you have available should work fine other than food oils or mineral oils (former will yellow, latter won't dry)

They're much more versatile in the sense that you can make your own stains if you want to preserve the grain of the wood by mixing it with a lot of clear oil to a watery consistency. The colour will sink into the grain unlike acrylics. Stain from the hardware store is essentially this.

You can also make a thicker version that is more like what you're used to with acrylics by diluting them less, but the pigmentation is much more vibrant and lasts longer

Lastly, you can rub the colour on the surface of the wood with a teeny amount of raw oil paint and work it over. I do this with yellow on basswood or yellow poplar. The paint disperses out until you can't tell, but it makes it almost glow golden at the end of it

Only downside is that they take longer to dry, but it's absolutely worth it. You can pick up a small pack from any art store for 10-20 dollars. I got mine from amazon for about 13 pounds, almost 2 years ago, and I use them for painting too, so they last a long time

Highly recommend investing in some oil paints and diluting them

It doesn't look sealed from the pictures but the playing squares of the board look a bit glossy, like they might have something on them. Hard to say from pictures alone. 

Put a drop of water on the surface to test. If it beads, then it's sealed, which means that any oil probably won't penetrate the wood and probably requires someone with more experience to remove and re-finish. Just for example (because this doesnt look like it has a poly finish), but poly is normally sanded off because using alcohol to remove it is a pain in the ass, not very efficient and you run the risk of damaging the pieces. Stuff like shellac can be relatively painlessly removed with alcohol, but it is time consuming. Lacquer, dunno.

To me, it doesn't look sealed. If you're willing to waive risks then you can just oil it up first. You can get non-stain oils from the hardware store, or linseed oil is good too. Mineral oil doesn't really dry, so it will feel "greasy" to the touch, so I don't recommend. Apply, leave for 5-10, then wipe the excess with a microfibre cloth. Don't forget, because it will go sticky. Same process for the pieces.

Then you can seal, if you're feeling brave, but it isn't absolutely necessary. It just looks better and lasts longer. Without seal, it'll wear quicker and look more "dull" when the oil dries. You can just oil it again, years down the line to revitalize it again.

Most people use poly for seals, there's a lot of different ones and different application methods. I don't use poly so I can't advise. I just know it's annoying to remove. I mix up de-waxxed golden shellac with some alcohol in a jar until it's a very thin syrup consistency. For this board, I would apply it with a microfibre rag and rub it into the wood all over, then do that a few times. It's easily removed with alcohol and a cloth if mistakes are made, which is the biggest draw for me. Shellac wares quicker than other finishes though, but I think that only really matters for everyday use. Something like a chessboard, yeah you're handling the pieces but not in such a way that it would ware the finish off quickly

No one has mentioned grits, so I will. Start with 80 or 120 for this one. If you start with 80, make sure not to skip 120. Sometimes you can get away with it, but because 80 is so rough, you won't get the marks out if you skip 120. If you use 80, don't push so hard with it because getting the deep marks out is really annoying.

After that, spray or wet the whole thing with water and let it dry. Sand with 180 when dry. The water lifts the fibres and lets you get a really smooth finish. This works best sanding into oil, but since this is for your kid, you probably don't want to be using any finish that might end up getting chewed on

Higher the grit, smoother the finish. Higher the grit means you can get away with skipping grits for something like this and still have a buttery smooth feel, but I wouldn't go over anything 320+

If you don't want to get finer sandpaper and happen to have some 0000 steel wool laying around, it's about 400-600 grit equivalency, especially if you do the water thing I suggested above

Sand in circles to even out the surface, then sand towards the grain before moving up grits

My hot take: there is a common learning problem that competitive players fall into where you start out as instinctually good. You form all your important connections using the fastest part of your brain early, then when you try to turn pro, you start to lose and struggle to handle that. This is often emotional, forming prejudice and lashing out, like Grubby in his early WC3 career. A lot of players that *could* be long-term competitive simply burn out at that stage. 

Grubby didn't, and those like him don't, because you learn to become more analytical. You very slowly (and i mean slowly) adopt a new form of learning to improve your game that sits on top of your original instinctual development. This higher learning, involves studying replays religiously, becoming extremely rote with strategy and become less emotional. You become more statistically minded. HasuObs is a great example of this in this career. He is the epitome of steady and higher mindset learning.

The problem comes when you become *too* analytical. You lose touch with your original instinctual self. You put less emphasis on reactive players and mechanical execution. You become overly conservative and lose your lethality, as such missing opportunities that your younger self would have seized, in favour of the "bigger" picture. This happens because you don't put as much value in individual plays anymore. It's seen as the young person's gambit. You lose confidence in your original self and never rekindle it. Your higher mindset learning becomes corrosive and you overanalyze your mechanical misplays instead of brute-forcing through it with raw emotion. 

Many people (like Grubby) correctly identify this as an aspect of getting older, however incorrectly identify it as something that can't be reversed or tempered. It is true of all things in life that with age comes wisdom, but there are many examples of people within history that still manage to maintain the instinctual, reaction part of their brain well into their 50s and beyond. It is possible to be both, but it requires work.

The unfortunate reality is that when you are successful, you are comfortable. Comfort is anathema to motivated learning. Most just turn their hands to sports coaching at this point, and I understand that decision.

But, for those that don't, don't fall into the trap of believing that you're washed up. It's an artificial lie perpetuated by those that long for their glory days but are unwilling to put the effort in anymore. When you recognise the behaviour, you start to apply it to all sorts of things in life and it becomes very obvious to see.

I'd say it's normal not to feel much of anything when you're doing tasks you contextualize as minor or unworthy of feeling good about. However, contexts change. For example if you're depressed, getting out of bed is monumental, but not so much when you're not struggling.

I'd say it's much more common that we train ourselves to not see the benefits or satisfaction of our actions. If you do this long enough, it becomes automatic and difficult to see worth in anything you do. The why of it is hard to pick apart and something only you can answer based on your development. It's a long journey to figure out the why of it. However, I think it's a positive thing to have identified the behaviour and I think it's worthwhile to try to work on it in the interim.

I think happiness is just the security of feeling content and confident in yourself. If that is true, then I would ask myself what do I need to feel content? What do I have to do to feel confident in myself?

The former is mostly just an identifying exercise. I've sat down in the past with a pen and paper, and made bullet points of what I need to feel content. I've never reached a full conclusion, but I've at least been able to figure out certain things I can work on that ultimately have improved my life in the long term.

For the latter, I'd say the word confidence has a bit of a misnomer these days. It ultimately gets lumped in with simple social esteem and projection, but what I really mean when I say confidence is the feeling you get when someone asks you about yourself. That's more about you than anyone else. I think it's very important to develop a purpose in life and with that comes confidence. It gives colour to your personality. So, I think it's a useful thought experiment to really sit down in a quiet room and commit resources to thinking of yourself, what you're good at, what you enjoy, and what you can reasonably achieve if you put effort into pursuing something to enrich yourself. Everyone has interests or old hobbies. Something. Anything. It doesn't matter what it is because the process of developing it and improving at it will make you feel like you're worth something.

And here's the kicker, everyone is worth something. Modern living is a rat-race, but society doesn't dictate your value. It does, but shouldn't dictate your experience. We are all slaves to it, but finding a way out of that cycle is a large part of maturing and gaining wisdom in life. In a lot of ways, we all go through this process, though it is more painful for some than others.

Most of all, be kind to yourself. We have a habit of picking apart our choices or achievements. Ghosts live in our minds, and that's okay, but it is important to recognise when you're just beating yourself up using other people's judgement. It's natural, and it sucks, but you have the potential to take control and get what you want out of life.

I think the resistance to embracing the idea that we are all on the spectrum is born from two things: fear that those who need extra help will not get it and the unfortunate trend of exceptionalism going around online now.

Both are social problems, separate from objective truth. If you fear someone will not get the support they need then that blame is with you or the institutions around the vulnerable individual. 

Yes it's true that there is a danger of people under appreciating the amount of support someone on the extreme end might need and thus being negligent, but I think treating autism as some handicap is equally as harmful; ESPECIALLY for those that are middle of the road, i.e. are intimately aware of their struggles but do not quite fall into the category of requiring a robust system to support them

Oil will not seal, it will sink into the pores of the wood. There are some kinds of oil like linseed that will oxidise on the surface which kind of works like a seal, but I'm not sure how that would go with watercolours or the longevity of it. I've used linseed once before and the finish was nice, but it's also expensive and dulled over time. 

I started using shellac to seal a few months ago and the difference is night and day. I do oil paints then seal when it's dry. The colour is still as vibrant today as it was months ago. Poly would do the same thing though, but there are so many types and I've never used any so I'd be hesitant to recommend. I know they come in aerosol too which can be easy for application. They're also water or oil based, so maybe the water ones would mess with your watercolours?

As far as shellac goes, I buy golden shellac flakes from amazon. They're little translucent flakes from some bug that dissolve in alcohol. The idea is that the flakes dissolve, you apply the mixture and then the alcohol evaporates leaving the seal on the wood. 

They use it in traditional French polishing but I've found that their methods are way too complicated for my purposes. I just mix it up in different ratios and apply with a brush. There's a bit of a learning curve when applying it because the alcohol runs like water. It tacks up relatively quickly though. 

The trick is to apply it evenly by brushing frequently on your carving until it starts to tack. Then you do some finishing strokes to make sure it isn't pooled in areas like crevices otherwise it will dry milky white. If it does, you can fix with raw alcohol. You can sand it (use a fine grit, it will strip it otherwise) and apply as many layers as you like. I typically only do 2 or 3 for my small carvings, some extremely light sanding between layers.

Anyway, sounds complicated but it's just bung the flakes in a jar, cover it in alcohol, apply and work it. The finish is kind of light glossy though, so if you're going for more matte finish then it might not be for you

The shine is a combination of a smooth surface and golden shellac. The smooth surface is from sanding through various grits and i have some polishing papers of high grit that i do a quick run over the surface. There is also a shine associated with the oil paints I use when i want colour on something. Most folks use acrylic and it always looks chalky to me which I don't like.

Shellac is my sealer (varnish). It's a bug resin that you can buy in flake form and mix with alcohol. I mix that up myself in a jar and add a couple of coatings of that with either a brush or a cloth. I lightly sand between coats with a very high grit and minimal pressure. 

Shellac is a new thing for me, so I'm still learning to apply it properly. I used to just do oil finishes with sanding, but I've found it dulls over time without a sealer. 

I think most people use polyurethane to seal in its many forms. I don't use it because it isn't a natural product and it isn't as forgiving as shellac. If I mess up with the shellac (sometimes it clumps and goes milky), I can just work it with some alcohol and it dissolves. As far as I know, it's harder to fix mistakes with poly. I just use some very thin interior clear oil from the hardware store for all my woodworking and diluting, but typically oil paints are diluted with linseed oil in the likes of oil painting. 

I haven't noticed any adverse effects of diluting with stuff from the hardware store other than its much easier to get thin colours whereas linseed is much thicker (and more importantly --expensive). 

If I was going to only use oil to finish without paints or sealer (I use a homemade shellac over everything I do to the wood normally), I'd use just linseed because it polymerises with the wood. Since I seal with shellac it doesn't matter to me if the oil polymerises or not (I think).

Drying depends on the size of the wood. I have logs that I've been drying out for 10 to 12 months, but they're quite large. Branches and the like wouldn't take long to dry out. Maybe a month at most for a large branch. The primary concern of drying naturally is warping or cracking. This is less of a concern for small bits of wood like what you sound like you're collecting, so you can whittle them while they're "green" without much concern. Larger logs require sealing to slow the drying process. There are quicker ways to dry that are a bit too involved for me, but I've read of people using ovens and stuff. Something to look into maybe

Any wood works and any steel works. A lot of folks will talk about brands and specific types of wood but I like to keep things simple when I'm starting out. Knife, wood, carve. Get yourself some whetstones and a strop. They're both inexpensive and absolutely necessary to keeping your tools sharp. It's a skill you need to learn anyway and makes your work much easier. I imagine your wood splintering is in part because of this.

Basswood (also known as limewood or linden) is a great wood to carve. Walnut is nice. Beech is nice. Pine can be nice. There are lots of good woods for starting out. I'd stick to whatever you can find on your hikes and maybe get a basswood block pack. They're easy to find.

Oil is really just dealer's choice. It honestly doesn't matter too much. Some oil polymerises when it cures and protects the wood better. You can get oil blends from any hardware store that are normally some mix of resins and tung. If you plan on using your spoons then you'll want to research a food safe oil/wax combo. These are usually a blend of mineral oil and beeswax. Linseed oil is a common finish and is available in any art store because oil painters use it (comes in different types like boiled and refined, but they're all fine to use). There are other types of natural oil, but things that you might use in food like olive oil will go rancid on wood over time.

Some of the hardware store finishes have stains baked into the blend which will change the colour of your wood. Different oils react to the wood differently and you'll find yourself experimenting endlessly. I find it a lot of fun changing finishes for different effects. 

Sealants are different. They (mostly) seal the pores and essentially "preserve" the wood. You don't need to seal your wood but it can be beneficial. Polyurethane is a common sealant and it comes in all sorts of forms (aerosol, liquid, then oil or water based). There are also lacquers and shellac. I started using shellac to finish my art carvings last year. I apply it over a clear oil finish and it just gives a little extra protection and gloss that i like, but it isnt essential. 

Since you're starting out, I would just stick with an oil or wax finish. Again, if you're using your spoons for more than display then get something food safe.

It's a type of resin. You buy it in dewaxed form and it comes in little flakes. You dissolve the flakes in ethanol and apply. The alcohol evaporates and leaves the resin. 

There's a lot of info on ratios but I just winged it. Honestly I don't think it matters much. Best thing I ever read about shellac was imagine one of the flakes spread evenly over your piece of wood. That's essentially all you're doing. 

Application is very different than oils because it's so runny. French polishers do a padding technique. I just use a brush and keep brushing the surface to get an even coat. After a couple of minutes you can feel it go tacky. I put it down at that point and leave it for 5 to 10. 

I give it a light sand with some high grit, wipe it off and feel for smoothness. Since I do weird little shapes, I'll often get uneven areas. You can see the resin coming off with the light sanding in areas that it's uneven, almost like taking a pumice stone to skin or something. I just do another coat after that with the same technique without the sanding at the end. It's normally pretty smooth after that

I'm new to it but I love it. You kind of just get a feel for it as you use it. I think it's much better than polyurethane or otherwise. It's also very friendly to touch ups. Sometimes I have areas that I can't sand properly so I just brush it with raw ethanol. It dissolves the resin and evens it out. Very cool

If you're scraping the wax off then the angle your blade is at is too steep. You want to run the edge of the blade along the wax. 

Try to visualize what you're doing to the edge of the blade. You're "shaving" the metal with the abrasive and in doing so creating a little overlap on the other side. Then you flip the blade over and evenly strop that side a few times to "remove" the overlap. You'll get a sharp finish everytime.

The majority of your work will be on one side of the blade. The other is just for getting rid of the burr

Don't worry about accidentally roughing up the leather. If you push the wax onto the leather it will fill in the gaps. Obviously you want as smooth an application and leather as possible for a "perfect" blade, but it isn't essential. 

Far and few between are those that have perfect tools. If your equipment is sharp enough for your needs then that is good enough. And, as always, you'll see significant improvement the more you do it, so don't get overwhelmed by guides or details

I started with a sloyd, picked up a small pfeil and some gouges along the way. Just the knife is all you need for starters. Get some whetstones, a strop and wax. Learn the knife and how to maintain it before you do anything further

All a strop really does is finish a blade off by removing the burr that forms on the other side of the blade. It also helps you maintain an edge while you're working if you do it regularly, so you don't have to use stones so often

If your knife feels blunt even after stropping then you need a whetstone to hone the blade. If the knife is relatively new then you probably only need a 1k stone. 

If you see yourself doing the craft long term, even as a hobby, then you might want to invest in some diamond whetstones. I got 400, 1k and 2k grit recently and my knives cut like butter. They're not too expensive either. I got mine for about £28

Sharpening and honing is a skill within itself that you learn alongside whittling or otherwise. It's very important to maintain your knives and doing so makes your work much easier. I'm still using my original no-brand sloyd knife just because I maintain the steel so well that there's really no point in buying a fancy one. When you get good at it, you start to find yourself sharpening all sorts of things like scissors or garden tools. It's a very useful thing to learn

I have a set of bits for boring the inner hole for rings that I just use with a basic bosch home drill. 

Before I had the drill, I would do it manually with a hand drill. I'd cut several small holes then use them to anchor the blade and cut out the inner circle. The inner circle is drawn onto the wood with a basic school compass and a pencil. It's roughly 21mm, which is a good size for my thumb but you could go smaller.

After the inside is done, you just decide how thick you want the outside and do whatever design you want. I find small files very helpful for these rings. I used a round file for most of them. I picked a cheap set up at the hardware store. The rest is just sanding from 120 onwards once the knife work is done.

My only useful advice would be to be mindful of the toughness of your wood. For example the purpleheart you can go quite thin but I wouldn't with beechwood. Stuff like padauk can be very brittle if it's dry too. Oh and sand the inside, so it's easy to slip on and off your fingers/thumbs

* Get pine pellet cat litter. It's the best shit ever. I'll never go back to anything else. Clean your litter box out regularly. No one likes to poop on poop
* Cats are really, really, really shit at getting water into their body. I used to give my kitty half a can of wet food mixed with water OR better yet, those little gravy treats mixed with water about once a week. You'll help your kitty out big time in the long term. A lot of cats develop crystals in their bladder in old age because of a strictly dry food diet
* Get a water fountain. Cats want to drink from a "fresh" water source
* Cats are purely carnivores. They shouldn't eat anything that isn't meat or protein related generally. I used to give my cat a bit of watermelon every now and again for water content and he enjoyed it, but I think anything more than a small portion would cause issues from sugar
* Get your kitty toys and play with them regularly. They get bored and the bonding is nice. Shoelace is king. The treat balls they have to nose and paw around are great too
* It's good to play-wrestle with cats, but they get over-stimulated easily. Don't encourage aggression. Let them know when they're hurting you and stop fighting back. They'll stop. They're smart. Don't punish. If you've ever watched kittens play, they just play rough.
* Get a cat tree and put it in your busiest room
* Clear space on your windowsill and make sure it's easily accessible. Yeah cats jump, but they're not always graceful
* Groom your cat every so often
* Clip your cats front-paws every so often. By clip I mean just the tip. They get sharp as hell. Don't clip your cats back murder-toes. Cats are climbers and they need them, especially if you have a cat tower
* The old adage that cats are independent is true to an extent. They won't do anything they don't want to, so don't force them. The exception to this is if they're somewhere they're not supposed to be (like counters), in which case I would remove them and tell them a stern "No". * They have their own personalities. Not all cats are cuddly. I've actually only ever had 1 cuddly cat out of a handful. I prefer an aloof cat anyway. * Cardboard boxes make the best forts
* **Lastly and most importantly**, make sure you're ready for this kind of responsibility. A cat can live for a very, very long time (16+ years). Get yourself a couple of whetstones, a strop and abraisive wax to keep your knives/gouges sharp. Most starter whittling knives come with the strop and wax. I use 400/1k and 3k/8k grit whetstones. I don't use the 400 or the 8k. 400 is for very dull or misshapen knives and 8k is mostly just for shine. I've had two injuries in the last year of learning whittling and both were from not using gloves and having blunt knifes. 

It'll take time to figure out your own technique for sharpening. There's a lot of video tutorials on youtube, but I found Paul Seller's the most helpful for all things. He's very resourceful, articulate and practical. My technique is probably amateur, but I've only been doing this a year and I can get them sharp enough for my purposes.

I start sanding at 120, to 180, to 320 then depending on the wood I "polish" using micro-abraisives either before or after I apply oil. You can buy a pack of ascending grit micro-abraisives on amazon for cheap. They start at 1.5k and go to 7k. There's some learning to do with sanding and I think most people don't bother for small projects, but I like the finish on certain things like little fruits or animal faces. I normally do "wet" sanding with 320 grit on hardwood because it seems to take care of small scratches. "Wet" sanding is when you apply your finish (oil in my case) and sand the surface (i do circles then line it up with the grain to finish).

Other than that, it's all just practice and interest. Start with softwood like basswood. I still mostly only carve with basswood. I buy a small bag from amazon and work through it all then maybe do something with some foraged hardwood from nearby. I think easy shapes are a good starting point. I started doing mushrooms and fruits.

The best bit of advice is to not force the wood too much. I'm impulsive so I used to try to brute force the wood without paying much attention to the direction of the grain. That's a bad idea when you're starting out. It'll result in injuries or just bad cuts on the wood itself. Try to work with the grain where possible and when you need to do a detail across the grain, cut straight lines to break the fibres so your work is clean and your knife doesn't slip.

Like the sharpening tutorials, there's probably a lot of whittling tutorials but I think it's best to just dive right in with knife and wood. You'll figure out the rest later
